newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices fall, soybeans higher on exports.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall, soybeans higher on exports.

text.p: Oil prices fell Monday as two refineries came back on line after maintenance and soybean prices jumped on strong demand for exports.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline led oil prices lower. December unleaded gasoline fell 1.15 cents to 65.77 cents a gallon.

Sun Co. said it restarted its 85,000 barrel a day unit at the Marcus Hook, Pa., refinery following maintenance. Sun said its 80,000 barrel a day crude distillation unit will return to service later in the day.
That news was enough to prompt selling, along with weakness in gas oil futures on London's International Petroleum Exchange, traders said.

Gas oil, the European equivalent of heating oil, was hit by news that barges set to deliver a record amount of gas oil were backed up in Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp, northwest Europe's oil and refining hub.
December heating oil fell 0.76 cent at 71.85 cents a gallon. December crude fell 29 cents to $23.88 a barrel.
But some traders cautioned against thinking oil prices were headed sharply lower.

The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries will meet next week to discuss keeping its production ceiling at 25.03 million barrels a day, a stance backed by OPEC President and United Arab Emirates oil minister Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad on Sunday.
But U.S. stocks of heating oil remain more than 10 percent lower than this time last year, with most all the shortfall in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.

"People are waiting for weather forecasts and stocks data. If you can't build stocks in the next two or three weeks you're heading for a very tight market this winter," said Bo van Wijk, vice president energy risk management at Swiss bank UBS in Zurich.
Soybean futures jumped after the Agriculture Department's weekly report showed export inspections set a record.
November soybeans closed up 12-1/4 cents at $7.11-1/4 at bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade. Soymeal and soyoil prices also posted sharp gains.
"They were record exports, the shipments were great," said Ron Kucha of Chicago trade house O'Connor and Co.
The department said 38.92 million bushels of soybeans were inspected for export at U.S. ports during the week ended Nov. 14, well above the highest industry estimates of 30 million.
The government said the total broke the prior week's record of 37 million bushels -- a new figure revised up from the 33.4 million bushels reported last Monday.
The strength in soybean exports comes despite protests in Europe and the United States last week over genetically modified U.S. soybeans.
Rumours that China was continuing to buy U.S. soymeal also added to positive sentiment, traders said.
Meanwhile, wheat prices fell after Egypt bought 600,000 metric tons of wheat from Australia, Argentina and France and none from the United States due to high U.S. prices.
December wheat fell 3-1/4 cents to $3.94 a bushel at the CBOT, and traders noted that prices had fallen on Friday on the likelihood that Egypt might buy non-U.S. wheat.
"That's what broke it Friday, we weren't competitive," said Skip Searcy of FIMAT Futures.
